name: NAD+
summary: A molecule cells use to make energy, given by IV drip or injection or taken by mouth hoping for more energy and slower aging; human evidence is minimal.
what_it_is: NAD+ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) is a molecule in the body's cells that takes part in energy metabolism. People try to raise their levels with NAD+ itself, given by IV infusion or injection, or with precursors taken by mouth such as nicotinamide riboside (NR) and nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN). In a small study, infused NAD+ was rapidly removed from the blood, probably broken down by enzymes such as CD38, with some passed in urine.

evidence.why: Human data on NAD+ itself are a pilot infusion study of 11 men and a small clinic chart review with no health outcomes; trials of oral precursors show higher NAD+ levels but unclear benefits.

status_us.label: Not FDA-approved; pharmacies may compound it
status_us.note: FDA lists NAD in Category 1 (under evaluation) of its interim policy for substances that are not part of an FDA-approved drug and have no applicable USP monograph, so state-licensed pharmacies may compound it while FDA decides. Oral NAD+-boosting compounds such as NR and NMN are used and studied as dietary supplements.

benefits.claim: Raised blood NAD+ during a 6-hour IV infusion in healthy men, but only after about 2 hours, because infused NAD+ was at first rapidly and completely removed from the blood (8 men on NAD+, 3 on saline)
Oral precursors such as NR and NMN can raise NAD+ in several human tissues and appear safe in trials so far, but whether this improves physical function is unclear

risks.risk: Discomfort during IV infusion: all 6 clinic clients given IV NAD+ in a small chart review had moderate to severe cramping, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fast heart rate or chest pressure, which stopped when the infusion ended and led them to slow it down; a 2019 pilot in 8 men reported no adverse events
Little safety information beyond the short term: human studies are small and brief

avoid_if: Liver or kidney disease (excluded from the infusion study; ask a clinician)

labs.why: No evidence-based monitoring exists; the small infusion studies checked liver, kidney and other blood markers and found no meaningful changes.

studies.title: A Pilot Study Investigating Changes in the Human Plasma and Urine NAD+ Metabolome During a 6 Hour Intravenous Infusion of NAD+
studies.people: 11 healthy men aged 30 to 55 (8 NAD+, 3 saline)
studies.finding: Blood NAD+ did not rise for the first 2 hours, then peaked at the end of the infusion; breakdown products rose and some NAD+ was passed in urine. No adverse events were reported, and some authors were linked to an IV NAD+ clinic.

studies.title: Intravenous infusion of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) versus nicotinamide riboside (NR): a retrospective tolerability pilot study in a real-world setting
studies.people: 14 wellness-clinic clients (6 IV NAD+, 8 IV NR)
studies.finding: All NAD+ clients had moderate to severe symptoms during infusions, versus mostly mild tingling or cramping with NR; blood markers stayed stable. The review was small, uncontrolled and run by the clinic company.

studies.title: Dietary Supplementation With NAD+-Boosting Compounds in Humans: Current Knowledge and Future Directions
studies.people: Human trials of NR, NMN and related compounds
studies.finding: These supplements can raise NAD+ in several tissues and appear safe and tolerable, but evidence that they improve physiological function is unclear and most trials are small.

ask_your_clinician: Is there any evidence that NAD+ infusions would help the symptoms I want to treat?
What should happen if I get chest pressure, cramping or a racing heart during an infusion?
Would an oral precursor be a lower-risk option, and how would we judge whether it works?

notes_for_editor: Both human NAD+ infusion studies have commercial ties: some 2019 pilot authors were linked to an IV NAD+ clinic, and the 2026 chart review was run and funded by a wellness-clinic company. They disagree on tolerability (no adverse events versus symptoms in all six NAD+ clients), possibly because of infusion speed, which was not compared directly. FDA's list also puts NADH in Category 1 and a disodium salt of NAD in Category 3 (nominated without adequate support). The NAD+-booster review was read only as an abstract, and no source on oral NAD+ itself (as opposed to its precursors) was opened.
